Abstract
13
Background: The yearly number of publications in many fields, including research on
14
potential health effects of electromagnetic fields (EMF), has steadily risen, making
15
systematic reviews (SRs) increasingly laborious. Automating the title and abstract
16
screening phase using large language models (LLMs) is a promising solution. However,
17
prior studies have underexplored structured LLM workflows, including explicit reasoning
18
outputs, few-shot prompting, and task-decomposition.
19

Workflows were designed to elicit PECOS-wise decisions with explicit reasoning, and
23
record-level verdicts were derived using deterministic decision rules.
24
Results: Three workflows, one based on an open-source (llama3.3:70b) and two based
25
on proprietary LLMs, achieved high sensitivity while substantially reducing manual
26
screening effort. The proprietary LLM gpt-4.1-mini embedded in a few-shot workflow with
27

28
with a workload reduction of 80.4% (95% CI: 63.7%–90.5%) at an approximate batch API
29
cost of $1.0 per 1,000 records. Overall, small “mini” models performed competitively,
30
demonstrating cost-efficient and resource-friendly applicability.
31

32
explicit PECOS-wise reasoning can achieve near-human sensitivity while substantially
33
reducing manual screening effort. These findings provide a transparent and versatile
34
framework for AI-assisted literature screening in systematic reviews, although further

Background
44
Systematic reviews (SRs) are the gold standard for evidence synthesis and are widely
45
used to assess the effectiveness of interventions or the association between exposures
46
and specific outcomes. To formulate a focused research question and define eligibility
47
criteria, SRs typically rely on structured frameworks such as P(opulation)-I(ntervention)-
48
C(omparator)-O(outcome)-S(tudy type) or, for exposure-focused reviews, PE(xposure)-
49
COS [1]. These frameworks operationalise inclusion and exclusion decisions and
50
therefore directly govern the literature screening process.
51
In the multi-stage SR workflow, potentially relevant records are first retrieved from
52
bibliographic databases using deliberately broad search strategies designed to maximise
53
coverage of the underlying PE/ICOS question (hereafter referred to as PECO[S]). Titles
54
and abstracts (TiAb) are then screened, usually independently by two human reviewers,
55
to assess compliance with predefined eligibility criteria, with discrepancies in decisions
56
resolved through discussion, or, if needed, adjudication by a third reviewer. Records
57
passing this initial stage undergo full-text

eligibility criteria, with discrepancies in decisions
56
resolved through discussion, or, if needed, adjudication by a third reviewer. Records
57
passing this initial stage undergo full-text retrieval and a second eligibility assessment
58
before inclusion in the final evidence base. Subsequent steps include risk-of-bias
59
assessment, data extraction, evidence synthesis, and certainty evaluation. While, in
60
principle, several of these stages could be supported by artificial intelligence (AI), the TiAb
61
screening phase is widely regarded as the most promising target for automation, offering
62
substantial potential workload reduction without compromising methodological rigour [2].
63
Whether AI can fully replace human reviewers at any stage of the SR process remains
64
debated and is likely to depend on future methodological and technological advances [3].
65

4

At a minimum, however, AI-based tools have demonstrated considerable potential to
66
meaningfully reduce human screening effort [4].
67
Over the past two years, numerous studies have investigated the application of
68
generative pre-trained transformer (GPT)-based large language models (LLMs) to TiAb
69
and full-text screening tasks. Across this literature, the central challenge has consistently
70
been achieving an acceptable trade-off between sensitivity and specificity, and thereby
71
meaningful workload reduction. While some studies report very high sensitivity and
72
specificity for selected SR datasets, performance often degrades for other datasets,
73
where high sensitivity can only be achieved at the expense of specificity and limited
74
workload savings [5-7]. In addition, performance gains in some studies rely on dataset-
75
specific prompt refinement or decision-threshold tuning (e.g., Tran et al. [6]), highlighting
76
potential challenges in achieving consistent performance across heterogeneous
77
systematic reviews. Although post hoc optimisation of prompts, decision rules, or
78
inclusion thresholds has been shown to improve performance retrospectively, robust
79

across heterogeneous
77
systematic reviews. Although post hoc optimisation of prompts, decision rules, or
78
inclusion thresholds has been shown to improve performance retrospectively, robust
79
demonstrations of stable performance across independent datasets and diverse research
80
questions remain limited [6-10].
81
Regarding workflow design, many previous studies have relied on instructive zero-shot
82
prompts that require the LLM to return a single overall verdict, typically “accept/include”
83
or “reject/exclude”, and in some cases an additional “unknown” option, based on review-
84
specific eligibility criteria provided in the prompt [6, 8, 9, 11, 12]. Some studies additionally
85
required the model to provide a brief justification for its decision [6, 10].
86
Beyond a single overall decision, several approaches instead elicited PECO-wise
87
judgements. These were obtained either through parallel queries, resulting in multiple
88

5

LLM calls per record [6], or jointly within a single call [13-16]. Other studies moved away
89
from binary decisions altogether and required the LLM to output numerical relevance
90
scores (e.g., 1–5, 1–10, or 1–100), enabling post hoc adjustment of recall–specificity
91
trade-offs via threshold tuning [5, 7, 17].
92
The most frequently explored variable across prior work has been the choice of the
93
underlying LLM. Both proprietary and open-source models have been evaluated,
94
sometimes in direct comparison [5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13], with GPT-4o (OpenAI) achieving the
95
strongest performance in most studies, with one notable exception [12]. Additional
96
strategies explored the inclusion of majority voting across multiple LLMs [7] and
97
collaborative reviewer–adjudicator setups involving multiple LLM instances [10]. Overall,
98
LLM-based approaches have consistently outperformed traditional machine-learning
99
classifiers for TiAb screening [10, 13].
100
Despite the rapid pace of model development, relatively few studies in biomedical and
101
clinical SR automation have evaluated LLMs released after GPT-4o. Moreover, although
102
Chain-of-Thought–invoking prompt modifications

model development, relatively few studies in biomedical and
101
clinical SR automation have evaluated LLMs released after GPT-4o. Moreover, although
102
Chain-of-Thought–invoking prompt modifications have been explored in some studies [8,
103
10], and requesting explicit rationales has potentially served as an analogous mechanism
104
to improve performance [6, 10, 13, 15], reasoning models that natively perform such
105
reasoning have not yet been systematically examined in this context.
106
Taken together, the reviewed literature reveals several gaps in the systematic evaluation
107
of workflow design choices for LLM-based title/abstract screening:
108
• Although employed in individual studies, the performance impact of PECOS-
109
wise splitting of LLM calls (i.e., prompt partitioning or PECO-parallelisation,
110

6

e.g., Tran et al. [6]) has not been formally evaluated against single-call
111
approaches that require PECO-level judgements within one prompt (e.g., Li et
112
al., 2024 [13]).
113
• The effect of requiring explicit reasoning for each PECOS decision, compared
114
with providing PECOS judgements without reasoning, has not been
115
systematically assessed.
116
• Few-shot prompting has been explored in only a limited number of studies, and
117
systematic performance comparisons between few-shot and zero-shot
118
prompting strategies are scarce.
119
• While inclusion thresholds based on numerical relevance scores have been
120
explored [5, 7, 17], more flexible and deterministic decision rules based on
121
PECO-wise LLM judgements [13] have not been systematically tested for their
122
potential to optimise the trade-off between sensitivity and workload reduction.
123
• Variants of prompt chaining—where a task is decomposed into two or more
124
sequential subtasks—remain underexplored, with only a small number of
125
studies implicitly applying such strategies [10, 11] and even fewer directly
126
benchmarking them against single-prompt approaches [9].
127
• Tool-calling and agentic

with only a small number of
125
studies implicitly applying such strategies [10, 11] and even fewer directly
126
benchmarking them against single-prompt approaches [9].
127
• Tool-calling and agentic capabilities, such as incorporating external knowledge
128
sources (e.g., web or Wikipedia searches), have not been investigated as
129
potential means to augment domain-specific knowledge during screening.
130
• The use of synthetic title–abstract records during workflow development and
131
prompt optimisation has not been leveraged to enable systematic testing of
132

7

multiple workflow variants while minimizing the risk of overfitting and external
133
validation data leakage.
134
In this work, we address these gaps by systematically devising and comparing LLM-
135
based TiAb-screening workflows using the LangChain Python framework, testing models
136
of varying sizes from both open-source providers via Ollama and from a proprietary
137
source (OpenAI). We use a balanced set of 100 synthetic abstracts during a development
138
phase – analogous to a development set in machine learning – to select the most

promising workflows. The selected candidate workflows are then evaluated on three
140
complete, fully labelled SR datasets on potential health effects of radiofrequency
141
electromagnetic fields (RF-EMF), previously lead- or co-authored by our research team,
142
in an internal evaluation phase (analogous to a test set). Finally, one to two best-
143
performing workflows per model type are validated on external SR datasets, including
144
EMF and other research areas, serving as a hold-out set to assess generalisability
145
(Fig. 1).
146
Our primary aim is to maximise sensitivity for records ultimately included in the SR (i.e.,
147
after passing the full-text screening stage), minimizing the risk of missing relevant studies,
148
while allowing the exclusion of records that would have been discarded at full-text
149
screening. By separating inference from final decision-making, we provide tuneable
150
control over workflow outcomes.
151
Thus, our goal is to provide a reliable, reproducible, cost-efficient, and transparent
152
automation workflow that substantially reduces human screening workload while
153
maintaining high scientific rigour [18, 19].

Eligibility criteria

To develop prompts and test workflows, we used a single set of eligibility criteria adapted
237

Synthetic abstracts
243

14

We used synthetic abstracts to keep the internal evaluation datasets untouched during
244
workflow development. Because eligible studies are typically rare, using real SR records
245
during optimisation would reduce the number of eligible records available for subsequent
246
evaluation and lower statistical precision.
247
To generate synthetic abstracts, we used the SR1 eligibility criteria and prompted gpt-4o
248
(ChatGPT app) on March 24, 2025, to generate 25 eligible and 25 ineligible abstracts.
249
Among the ineligible abstracts, 10 were intended to fail three PECOS elements, 10 to fail
250
two elements, and 5 to fail one element. To diversify writing style and content, we
251
repeated the procedure with Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview 03-25 (Google AI Studio) on April 6,
252
2025 and generated an additional 50 abstracts using the same PECOS-failure distribution
253
(prompts in Supplementary File 1). This yielded 100 synthetic abstracts with a 1:1
254
eligible:ineligible ratio (Supplementary File 1).

Output constraints
260
To obtain consistent, parsable and fully comparable responses from all models, we
261
constrained output format by employing Pydantic BaseModel schemas and converting
262
them to JSON-style functions that can be attached to the LLMs as callable tools.
263
The standard output for a single-step workflow consisted of PECOS-wise reasoning and
264
decisions, i.e., a separate free-text reasoning field and a resulting decision for each of the
265

15

five PECOS elements (10 fields in total). For each PECOS decision, the LLM could return
266
True (include), False (exclude) or NotEvaluable (unsure) (Fig. 2). We introduced the
267
NotEvaluable option to capture records with too little or inadequate information for
268
evaluation (e.g., title-only records) or other issues (including technical/formatting failures).
269
The rationale was that records marked with one or more NotEvaluable decisions could
270
be flagged for manual review.
271
Variations of the standard output were reasoning-less schemas (five PECOS decisions
272
only; five fields total). A separate schema was used for two-step workflows: the first step
273

Discussion
883
Conducting systematic reviews is a rigorous and often resource-intensive process that
884
can be substantially alleviated through the incorporation of automation systems based on
885
large language models (LLMs). However, such systems must ensure high scientific rigour
886
and near-complete coverage of relevant evidence to reliably inform clinical or
887
environmental policy decisions. Accordingly, a sensitivity (recall) threshold of at least 95%
888
is commonly regarded as a minimum benchmark for the deployment of automated
889
screening systems [39].
890
Our external validation across eight largely independent SR datasets (830 eligible studies
891
out of 25,288 records) indicates that a few-shot prompting strategy with explicit PECOS-
892
wise reasoning, implemented using OpenAI’s gpt-4.1-mini and combined with the
893
sensitive R6 decision rule, meets this benchmark. The pooled sensitivity at 96.4% (95%
894
CI: 94.8%–97.6%) was likely conservative given several inconsistencies in the reference
895
ground truths. This level of sensitivity was attained alongside a pooled workload reduction
896
of 80.4% (95% CI: 63.7%–90.5%) and acquired at an average batch API

895
ground truths. This level of sensitivity was attained alongside a pooled workload reduction
896
of 80.4% (95% CI: 63.7%–90.5%) and acquired at an average batch API cost of
897
approximately $1.0 per 1,000 TiAb records. In practical terms, applying the Fs-M workflow
898
as an initial filtering step would reduce the proportion of records requiring manual
899
screening to an approximate average of 19.6% of the original retrieval, representing a
900
substantial reduction in human screening effort. Nevertheless, further optimisation will be
901
required to improve specificity without compromising sensitivity. The achieved sensitivity
902
closely matches the sensitivity of single human reviewers, reported at a median of 95%
903
[40], and of human dual-review at 97.5% (95% CI: 95.1%–98.8%; [41]). Given that

908

909

910

911

912

922

923

924

925

926

928

929

930

931

932

933

934
